## Open

### F-160 — The batch files cannot be used as the coverage map

> _2026-09-15 · cross-cutting · open_

The friction batches in dev/memory-migration/ account for 75 of the 77 legacy entries that reached
the memory tree: F-080 and F-081 were imported by another route, so diffing the batches against the
legacy document flags those two lines as missing when they are in fact covered. Compare the memory
files, which are the authority for coverage, not the batches. The same comparison surfaced a
duplicate: F-080 and F-090 are one legacy line imported twice, a day apart, for the same finding.

### F-161 — A terminal result can be another command's output

> _2026-09-15 · cross-cutting · open_

Twice in one session a run-in-terminal result came back with output that belonged to a different
command — a repo-wide grep returned a ranked search listing, and a targeted grep returned a diff of
decision.md. Both times the shape was plausible enough to act on, and the first one nearly produced
a wrong conclusion about what existed in the repo, because a search that silently returns nothing
looks like 'the string is absent'. Re-run any command whose output does not match the command, and
cross-check reachability questions with the workspace search tools instead of a single shell pipe.

### F-162 — A platform rule about CI triggering was assumed rather than verified

> _2026-09-15 · ci · open_

The CI design rested on a documented platform rule - that a push made with the workflow token does
not create a new workflow run - without checking it against the repository. In fact three metrics
commits had started runs, and the newest was held as `action_required`, asking a human to approve a
full re-run to commit two files. The user hit it, not the tests, because a wrong assumption about
_whether CI runs_ leaves nothing to fail. Lesson: for a trigger rule, read the run list after the
first real use.

### F-163 — Resolving a session by its title needs list --json

> _2026-09-15 · skills · open_

The session-analyser skill requires the user to name a session, but the text listing truncates each
title at roughly 72 characters, so a user answering with a paraphrase of the title (e.g.
"Requirement document for logging ideas") cannot be matched against it. Cost two clarification
round-trips. Lesson: run 'session-analyser list --limit 400 --json' and match on the full title
before asking, and when the cap is needed note that --limit-segments drops whole requests, so with
an average of ~180 segments per turn a partial budget covers only a couple of turns rather than
spreading evenly.

### F-164 — A writer whose CI branch was never exercised lost the PR comment

> _2026-09-15 · ci · open_

`ci-report.md` was written only when `GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` was unset, so every local check - the
fixture harness and the unit tests - took the branch that writes it while CI took the one that did
not. The workflow then uploaded no artifact and the comment was never posted, and because
`continue-on-error` covers the missing-artifact download, nothing failed. Lesson: when a helper
branches on a CI-only environment variable, exercise that branch in a test with the variable set;
`GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` now has a regression test that asserts both outputs.

### F-199 — A tool package cannot run itself from PATH

> _2026-09-19 · ci · open_

Seeding tools/blong-dev with '"test": "blong-dev test"' failed with '/bin/sh: blong-dev: not found':
the package does not depend on itself, so node*modules/.bin has no link, and the global bin is not
on a non-interactive PATH (every other package resolves it from its own node_modules). The lesson: a
package that \_is* the tool invokes its own entry - 'node bin/blong-dev.ts test' - which is also why
its ci-lint is 'tsc --noEmit' rather than 'blong-dev lint'.

### F-219 — get_errors missed a duplicate declaration that stopped the CLI from loading

> _2026-09-21 · cross-cutting · open_

Moving legName into lib.ts left the local copy in handlerProxy.ts. tsc through get_errors answered
'No errors found' for the file, while the spawned-CLI test failed with "SyntaxError: Identifier
'legName' has already been declared" - three failures that looked environmental (a dev server on the
port) and were not. Lesson: an import that clashes with a local declaration is only certain when the
module is loaded (or the file is linted through the package's ci-lint, which did catch a different
tsc error in the same change); after moving or renaming a symbol, run the affected suite rather than
trusting the editor's diagnostics.

### F-221 — A diagram baseline follows the run's log content, not just the code

> _2026-09-21 · cross-cutting · open_

Accepting the regenerated diagram baseline was not the end of it: the next plain run failed on a
two-pixel-taller render of the same diagram (a retry), and the framework realm's template baseline
had changed on its own, because the Observe page lists whatever the run logged (one extra 'call
error' row, and a 'Seen 2' where the committed baseline had 'Seen 1'). Two runs of each suite after
accepting were green, so the accepted baselines stand. Lesson: after regenerating a diagram or
viewer baseline, re-run the suite at least once before committing, and expect the change to include
rows and counts that the run, not the code, decided.

### F-244 — Documented modes drifted from the code in three places

> _2026-09-23 · docs · open_

Three documents stated the old behaviour and none of them is compiled, so nothing failed while they
drifted: `concepts/checkpoint.md` had a Modes table with a **Monitoring** row that never existed
(and said debug only records), `rationale/unified-handler-test.md` showed `createAttachCheckpoint`
returning `undefined` in production (it now always returns an attacher, so a dispatch can get
`decide`), and `demo/handler-test-poc/README.md` named the marker's type on `ILib.checkpoint`.
Lesson: when a mode's _semantics_ change, grep the docs for the table that states them — the docs
are the only place the old shape is still asserted, and the pre-commit lint does not read meaning.

### F-265 — get_errors said no errors for a file with an unbalanced brace

> _2026-09-26 · cross-cutting · open_

Editing core/blong-allure/lifecycle/allureSessionEnd.ts left a duplicated function header and an
unclosed promise body. The editor reported no errors for the file, while the run surfaced it as a
parse failure at the end of the file, and the suite that imports it failed every scenario. The
package lint and tsc caught it immediately once asked. Worth remembering: treat a package-level lint
or tsc as the check after an edit, not the editor's error list, which appears to lag for files that
were not already open.

### F-268 — A .js specifier in a source-consumed package passes tap and breaks the runtime

> _2026-09-26 · cross-cutting · open_

A `blong` realm stopped starting entirely, and every test suite stayed green — which is the part
worth remembering.

The cause was one import specifier. `core/blong-chain/index.ts` imported `progressTree` from
`./progress.js`, and there is no `progress.js`: the package is consumed as source
(`"exports": "./index.ts"`), so the runtime resolves relative specifiers against the real files and
found nothing (`ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`). The `.js` suffix looked right because the same file's
`./test-types.js` imports work — but those are `import type`, and type-only imports are stripped
before resolution, so they never ask for a file. Only value imports do.

tap hides the difference: a run under tap resolves `.js` to the `.ts` file, so the whole suite
passed while `blong` could not boot a realm. The lesson is to check the plain runtime, not only the
test runner, after touching an import in a package another package consumes as source.

Two packages needed their compiler options aligned with `core/blong-gogo` for `.ts` specifiers to be
legal at all: `allowImportingTsExtensions` with `noEmit`, `moduleResolution: bundler`,
`module: preserve`. `core/blong-chain` and `core/blong-allure` had `NodeNext` and emitted
declarations, which is why their authors had reached for `.js` in the first place.

### F-274 — One package's .ts imports break a consumer's build

> _2026-09-26 · cross-cutting · open_

CI failed building the ttk package with TS5097 (an import path can only end with .ts when
allowImportingTsExtensions is enabled) against core/blong-allure/index.ts, even though
blong-allure's own tsconfig sets that option. The mechanism is that packages in this repo export
their sources ("./index.ts"), so a consumer's tsc program compiles the dependency's files as if they
were its own and inherits their import syntax: blong-allure and blong-chain moved to .ts import
extensions in the same commit, and tools/blong-ttk was one of the few tsconfigs that had never set
the option, so its build broke while the changed packages and every other consumer stayed green. The
fix was one tsconfig — module preserve, moduleResolution bundler, allowImportingTsExtensions with
noEmit, and the declaration plus declarationMap pair removed because they cannot coexist with either
— after which ttk's type-check, lint, heft build and tests all pass. The lesson for the next import
sweep is to type-check the dependents of a package whose imports changed before finishing, which is
one local tsc run per dependent and much cheaper than a CI round trip; four other consumers
(core/blong-browser, core/blong-openapi, realm/blong-test, demo/blong-hello) still lack the option
and would break the moment their dependencies use .ts extensions.

### F-293 — Six doc pages and two skills described behaviour the code does not have

> _2026-09-27 · docs · open_

Verifying the five batch-5 posts before writing them turned up roughly twenty statements across the
Playwright concept and pattern pages, the three schema-sync tiers, the sessions concept page, two
realm READMEs, three skills and one RBAC diagram that the code contradicts: CI Playwright ports, an
unconditional webServer, a table cell id, a static-key section describing nothing in the repository,
a 'no manual SQL' claim that ignores procedure bodies, a deploy-time-only split that is
configuration, CRUD described as synthetic handlers when it is the generic exec, a type map wrong
about three types, an example whose table key cannot resolve under its own namespace, an adapter
method that is a realm handler, a realm example that does not exist, a refresh sequence naming a
grant that does not exist, and config that no caller passes to its handler. The pattern is the same
every time: the page was written from the design intent and the implementation moved, and nothing
re-reads it. That is the argument for treating 'Docs status: ready' as a claim to test rather than a
fact to quote, which is what the blog plan already says.

### F-295 — Nine areas recorded as ready needed roughly thirty corrections

> _2026-09-27 · docs · open_

Batch five and six verified eleven documentation areas before writing their posts and found about
thirty statements the code contradicts: the Playwright ports and webServer, a table cell id, a
static-key section describing nothing, no-manual-SQL, a deploy-time-only split that is

### F-306 — One new italic in a markdown file can light up every pre-existing one

> _2026-09-28 · cross-cutting · open_

Adding a sentence with _shape_ in italics to .github/skills/blong-model/SKILL.md turned a file with
two pre-existing markdownlint findings into one with ten: eight MD049 emphasis-style errors appeared
on lines I never touched, reporting expected asterisk and actual underscore. markdownlint resolves
the style from the first emphasis token in the file, so the new asterisk early in the document
became the expectation and every older underscore italic after it became a violation. The fix is one
word; the lesson is to match the italics the file already uses (the house style is underscore) and
to re-lint a markdown file after adding prose rather than assuming pre-existing findings are all it
has. It is also why the same edit looked harmless: the eight errors were in table cells and
paragraphs far from the change.

### F-308 — A glob inside a block comment ends the comment

> _2026-09-28 · cross-cutting · open_

A `/** ... */` doc comment that quotes a glob — the example shapes the merge helpers recognise —
contains `**/`, and the `*/` in it closes the comment early. The file then fails to parse, and the
syntax error points at the comment body, so it reads like a broken template literal or an unescaped
character in a string rather than a comment that ended two lines too soon. Quote the shape without
the trailing slash, spell it as prose, or keep the glob out of block comments; when a parse error
lands inside a doc comment, suspect the comment before rewriting the code.

### F-309 — The test job inherits a build-less cache written by another workflow

> _2026-09-28 · ci · open_

Nineteen packages came back with a module-not-found for the blong package dist types file while the
same suites passed locally, and nothing in the diff touched that package. The cause was not in the
code. The release flow on main and the pull-request Build workflow share one pnpm cache key, and the
Chromatic job of the release flow, which only installs, saved its filesystem under that key because
its save finished before the save of the job that runs rush rebuild did. Because a restore that hits
exactly suppresses the save, every later Build run in a different pull-request ref restored that
build-less archive, and the test job never builds. The diagnosis that settled it was the caches API:
the archive created_at matched the Post cache step of the Chromatic job to the second, while the
save of the builder completed a minute later. The same archive is what the release job packed from,
so blong 1.31.0 reached npm without dist. Lesson: when one missing module shows up in many packages
at once, look at what the run restored before reading the diff.

### F-310 — A repaired CI surfaced failures the broken runs could not reach

> _2026-09-28 · ci · open_

Fixing the cache took the Build workflow from 19 failing packages to 3, and then the re-run of the
same commit failed in two packages it had never reached before: the blong-access user editor
screenshot and the blong-realm digest page. Both look like regressions and neither is. The re-run
let packages that used to die at import run to completion for the first time in days, and what they
exposed is order dependence. The evidence for that reading: no functional change in the window
touches those paths (the blong-access and blong-core edits there are comments, the roleBit allocator
is protected by the unique constraint on access_role.roleBit plus the three attempts loop, and the
materialized path refresh deferral dates from 2026-08-12). What the suites depend on instead:
access.permission.list reads the roleBits and the action names of the user out of the materialized
core_path (access.effectiveRole and access.effectiveAction), so a race with the single refresh the
seed performs can drop an action from the paths (the 403 on blong.flow.find) and leave the effective
panel stale; and the create-test helper toggles the first pivot row rather than a named role, while
the bits of the seeded roles are handed out in whatever order the concurrent seed merges commit, so
which role is row zero changes between runs. Lesson: after unblocking a long-broken workflow, triage
the newly reachable failures separately from the ones that motivated the fix.

### F-311 — The report consolidation dropped the trace links

> _2026-09-28 · ci · open_

The consolidation of the CI reports onto Allure (93276a27, fb730360) removed the page whose Trace
column opened `https://trace.playwright.dev/?trace=...` and left only the bare `traces/<file>` name
plus a generic hint. The Allure attachment alone is not a viewer link, and nothing asserted either
one, so the loss was silent until a user missed it. Lesson: a feature that moves between report
formats needs an assertion on its observable, which is what `test/blong-ci-report` now has for the
summary row and `allurePublish.test.ts` for the attachment link.

### F-313 — A flag cleared by the repair is not a cross-process signal

> _2026-09-29 · cross-cutting · open_

The T-174 fix went in as a dirty flag plus a read-side fallback, and it passed every test that
existed because all of them ran in one process. The hole only shows up with two: process A rebuilds,
process B's merge commits while that rebuild runs, and A's rebuild deletes B's flag on its way out
without ever having seen B's edges — B's own drain then finds nothing owed, the edge is absent from
the flattened paths, and nothing is scheduled to put it back. The lesson is about the shape of
inter-process state rather than about this feature: a signal whose clearing is done by the party
that repairs it must be monotonic and written where the repair can compare it against what it read,
which is what the generation and covered counters do. It also cost a second lesson: all the existing
tests were in-process, so the missing coverage was the topology itself — the test that would have
failed is two coordinators over one database, and it now exists.

### F-316 — The ensure was ruled out of the transaction on a wrong premise

> _2026-09-29 · cross-cutting · open_

D-323 stated as a design fact that core.resource.ensure cannot join a caller's transaction because
core might be a separate service, and the session before this one built a workaround on that premise
(leaving the ensure outside, describing idempotency as the mitigation) instead of asking whether the
premise held. It did not: core is a library realm and its copy is in the calling process, so the
ensure is local and takes a transaction as soon as the mechanism to reach it is chosen. The cost was
a boundary written into code comments, a decision record and a close note, all of which had to be
rewritten. The lesson is to check the deployment fact a boundary claim rests on before building
around it, and — where the framework hides the fact (nothing said core is a library realm) — to
record it as a decision as soon as it is known, which is what this turn does.

### F-328 — A docs link must name its tier or only the build notices

> _2026-09-30 · docs · open_

Editing a page under `docs/blong/docs` needs relative links that name the tier: `./memory` for a
sibling in the same tier, `../patterns/memory` across tiers. A bare `../memory` from inside
`patterns/` resolves to `/docs/memory`, and nothing local notices — markdownlint and cspell do not
resolve links, so the page stays lint-clean while the route is wrong. Only `npm run build` reports
it, through `onBrokenLinks: 'throw'`, and finding it cost a full build cycle. The habit that avoids
it: a cross-tier link always has `concepts/`, `patterns/` or `rationale/` in it, so a relative link
without one of those words is either a sibling or a mistake.

### F-329 — A blog request names the feature, not the by-product

> _2026-09-30 · docs · open_

Asked for a blog article because a measurement came out well, I wrote about the measurement: 1431
words on three embedding models and the reranker, with the new ability as background. The user
wanted the opposite — the ability as the subject, the comparison as one small section — so the post
had to be rewritten and every claim in it re-verified. The lesson: a request for a blog article
names a feature, not the most interesting by-product of building it. Check the blog index for what
the feature still lacks first, and if the ability itself is not covered anywhere, that is the
article. A long-form measurement belongs in the plan that produced it, and in the blog only as the
section that says which choice could not be undone.

### F-332 — The test job restored a cache without docs/blong/.rush

> _2026-10-01 · ci · open_

Every `rush ci-test` in CI opened with "Error calculating the state of the repo:
docs/blong/.rush/temp/shrinkwrap-deps.json is missing" and then "This workspace does not appear to
be tracked by Git", which turns off the diffing, caching and change detection of the rest of the
run. The tests job never runs `rush install`, and the cache step lists nine category folders of
which docs was not one. Fixed by caching `docs/*/.rush`; docs/blong/node_modules (817MB, installed
by npm rather than through the pnpm store) is deliberately left out, because no job in the workflow
builds or tests that project.

### F-333 — A semicolon-chained ci-test script hides the first failure

> _2026-10-01 · ci · open_

tools/blong-log ran `blong-dev test;node --run storybook:test:ci` and core/blong-chain ran
`blong-dev test *.test.ts;./test-examples-ci.sh`; both scripts return the last command status, so a
red tap suite reported green whenever the second command passed. In blong-log that is the same leg
that was failing for another reason, which is how the masking stayed invisible. Both now capture
each status and exit non-zero if either command failed, while still running the second command,
which is what the chains were for.

### F-330 — One Playwright install covered three Playwright copies

> _2026-10-01 · ci · open_

The reusable workflow installed browsers with
`find . -path */node_modules/.bin/playwright -print -quit`, which resolved to demo/blong-marine
(@playwright/test 1.63, chromium 1243). The Storybook leg of tools/blong-log launched the
`playwright` copy that @storybook/test-runner resolves for itself, pinned at 1.60.0 in the
shrinkwrap, so it needed chromium_headless_shell-1223 and died with the message that the executable
does not exist, before its first test. The test job sets PLAYWRIGHT_SKIP_INSTALL=1, so nothing
installed at test time and the miss was fatal. Lesson: three Playwright versions in one workspace
are three browser revisions, and an install that picks one of them by `find -quit` is a lottery.
Fixed by pinning playwright and playwright-core to 1.63.0 through globalOverrides (10 insertions, 39
deletions in the lock) and by a per-leg preflight in blong-dev.

### F-342 — The repo holds stale autostash entries that a bare stash pop applies

> _2026-10-04 · cross-cutting · open_

The blong repo carries several stale autostash entries left by interrupted rebases (the oldest from
April). A bare git stash pop applies one of them to the working tree: it wrote conflict markers into
the root .github/memory files, put them in UU state and made memory check report 244 errors. Never
run a bare git stash pop here; name the stash, or compare a baseline with cp and git show HEAD:path
instead. Recovery when there is no MERGE_HEAD but UU paths: git checkout --ours then git reset,
which keeps the local side.

### F-424 — rush update --full re-resolves the lockfile and breaks the deployed suite

> _2026-10-07 · ci · open_

Running `rush update --full` to repair the store passes `--no-prefer-frozen-lockfile` and
`--config.resolutionMode=highest`, so pnpm re-resolves every range: typebox went from 1.1.8
to 1.3.36, which no longer exports `Type.Awaited`. That run then failed on the native build of
node-rdkafka and left the rewritten lockfile in place. Image and artifacts are built from that
lockfile, so every tenant pod of the suite started, logged its adapters as ready and died inside
`Registry._validations` with `TypeError: Type.Awaited is not a function` at
`core/blong-mock/index.ts:330`, while the operator pod stayed up — the symptom looks like a broken
build prune or a missing dependency, not like a resolution drift. Read the previous container log
(`kubectl logs <pod> --previous`) to see it; the current attempt only shows the crash loop. Fix:
`git checkout HEAD -- common/config/rush/pnpm-lock.yaml`, then a plain `rush update`, which
reconciles the intended change and keeps the pins. Lesson: never reach for `--full` on this host; a
lockfile that differs from HEAD for any reason other than the edit at hand is a regression until
proven otherwise, and `git status --porcelain` on the lockfile is worth one second before any
deploy.

### F-433 — The skill corpus outgrew the prompt budget, so eleven skills cannot load

> _2026-10-08 · skills · open_

The `skill` tool resolves a name only against the rendered skill index: `resolveSkillUri` in the
Copilot extension reads the chat variable that carries the prompt own skill section and collects the
entries that have a `<file>`, which is `jIe.getValuesInIndexFile("skills","skill","file")`. The
prompt builder inlines that section until a 15,000 character budget is spent (`let E=15e3`, and only
when the skill tool is enabled) and renders the remainder as a bare name list under a second 5,000
character budget (`let I=5e3`), and a bare name carries no `<file>` — so every skill past the cut is
advertised as loadable by name and cannot be loaded at all. The arithmetic now reproduces the
observed prompt exactly: the 33 workspace blocks total 22,063 characters in the builder own format,
the first 22 reach 14,744, and the 23rd, `blong-rest`, would reach 15,305, so the eleven that are
unreachable are `blong-rest` through `storybook-v10-setup` in alphabetical order. Order is workspace
root first, then the user-level `~/.agents/skills` library, then the bundled and extension skills,
and the budget is global rather than per root, so every `~/.agents` skill is name-only here as well
and the two roots cannot be balanced against each other. No setting exposes the size:
`chat.skillTool.enabled`, `chat.useAgentSkills` and `chat.agentSkillsLocations` exist, but none of
them sets it. The only supported way to keep a skill out of the block list is
`disable-model-invocation: true`, which is why the six wrapper skills in `~/.agents/skills` never
appear in a prompt. Repo-side levers are therefore to shrink the blocks — descriptions, or fewer
blocks by merging families, or a shorter `<file>` path — and the upstream fix is for the tool to
resolve from the discovered skill folders, which the extension already tracks, instead of from the
budgeted render. Measure with a YAML parse of the frontmatter: a regex that reads the `description:`
line alone under-counts every skill whose description is a multi-line YAML scalar, which is how this
was mis-measured twice.

### F-455 — A passing comparison never rewrites a stale baseline

> _2026-10-10 · cross-cutting · open_

Playwright updates a snapshot only when the comparison fails, so `--update-snapshots` (the default
mode) leaves a baseline that is stale but inside `maxDiffPixelRatio` exactly as it was. That is how
two commander explore shots kept a navigator tree listing the cluster namespaces the source had
stopped showing: the shot whose text had shifted 7% was rewritten, and the two whose stale rows sat
under 1% were not, so a regeneration looked complete while two thirds of it had not happened. Force
the rewrite with `--update-snapshots=all`, or delete the baseline file first. A golden that passes
is never inspected, which is what makes the tolerance silent rather than safe.

### F-462 — A rehomed operator left a workflow naming a Deployment that does not exist

> _2026-10-10 · ci · open_

The operator was rehomed out of the suite's namespace into its own (Phase 15 A, D-396), and the
kustomize workflow's two failure dumps went on naming `deployment/blong-suite-operator` in
`blong-suite`, where no such Deployment exists — the diagnostics written for the moment a job fails
printed nothing at all. The same job never watched `test/blong-int-kustomize`, the runbook it runs
end to end, so a change to its tree generation would not have triggered the job it is the subject
of. Both are fixed together. The lesson is the shape: a move has to be carried to the path filter
and the failure dumps as well, and neither of those is compile-checked — a grep for the old name
after a rename is what finds them.

### F-463 — The E2E job never collected the workloads that stalled

> _2026-10-10 · ci · open_

The kustomize E2E job has failed in every run it has had, each time one step further along: the
image build, then a strategic merge patch that named a Deployment in blong-suite that had moved to
blong-services, then the runbook's waits timing out on workloads that never became available. The
third failure could not be read at all, because the job collected the MySQL namespace and nothing
about the suite: no pods, no events, no node conditions, so a pod that never scheduled and a node
that stopped reporting look the same. Three runs of up to 31 minutes bought no evidence, and the fix
was to collect the state of every namespace a failure could be in rather than the one the
diagnostics script happens to know.

### F-464 — The image deployed a package whose export needs a build output

> _2026-10-10 · ci · open_

The framework image is built before anything else in the workflow, and its deploy copies each
package as it is: `@feasibleone/blong`'s `.` export resolves its `default` condition to
`./dist/types.js`, which `.gitignore` keeps out of the repository, so the deploy tree carried the
package's sources and no `dist/`. Every process then died on ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND — the operator and
all four suite pods crash-looped, the migrate Job errored, and the runbook waited out four progress
deadlines and a Job timeout before failing, because a container has no `--conditions=blong-dev` to
reach `types.ts` the way a development shell does; the trap only shows where the dev condition is
absent. The image now builds the package before deploying, verified by rebuilding it with `dist/`
moved out of the context. The class is worth remembering: a deploy copies files, an export names a
path, and the two only agree by accident when a build output happens to sit in the working tree —
which is exactly what a developer has and a runner does not.

### F-465 — A metric change broke the package that renders it

> _2026-10-10 · ci · open_

Changing what the CI report measures broke seven specs in `test/blong-ci-report`, the package that
renders it, because the specs pin the rendered strings and I ran only the specs of the package that
produces the numbers (`tools/blong-dev`), which stayed green. The cost was a red `build / tests` in
CI and a round of localising it. The lesson is mechanical: after changing a shared helper, run the
specs of every package that consumes it — `grep -rl` for the module is enough to find them — because
a renderer's expectations move with its input's meaning even when no signature changes.

### F-466 — A package has two legs, and the count line names one

> _2026-10-10 · ci · open_

Reading a package's count line in the rush test summary as the whole package is wrong:
`blong-commander: 16 passed, 0 failed (16 total)` is the tap leg, while the same package's
playwright leg failed on `explore.play.ts:402` and appeared in the log only as a test name in a
block above. I reported the package as passing when it had failed, and the correction came from
outside the evidence I had gathered. The guard is to read the FAILURE block of each package in that
summary, not only its counts line, and to treat a package flagged twice — once as failed to build
and once as a count — as two legs with two answers.

### F-473 — A kubectl spelling copied from cp to exec cost the diagnosis

> _2026-10-10 · ci · open_

A step that publishes the release's artifact died with
`error: the server doesn't have a resource type "default"`, which names neither the pod nor the
command. Two defects sat behind that one message, and the run could not say which fired. The first
is the command: `kubectl exec "default/$pod" -- cp …` used the `namespace/pod:path` form that
`kubectl cp` takes and `kubectl exec` does not — it takes a pod name, or `pod/name` — so kubectl
read `default` as a resource _type_ and answered exactly that. The step above uses the form
correctly for `cp`, which is where the spelling came from, and this repository's own
`test/integration/ci-diagnostics.sh` uses the right one (`kubectl exec -n "$NS" "$POD" -- mysql …`).
The second is the lookup: both `kubectl get pod -l app=artifact` calls trusted the kubeconfig's
_current_ namespace, which is shared state across a job's steps — on the machine this was diagnosed
on that namespace is `blong-suite`, and the bare lookup returns an empty list where
`kubectl -n default get pod -l app=artifact` returns the pod. An empty `$pod` produces the same
message as the wrong argument form, and no step switches the namespace, so which of the two failed
in CI cannot be settled from the log; both are fixed, every artifact command now names `default`,
and each step guards an empty `$pod` by listing the pods. The cost was the diagnosis rather than the
fix, and two lessons came with it: a bare `kubectl` command is not the same instruction in two
steps, and a message that fits two causes has to be narrowed by evidence rather than by preference.
Worth recording alongside: this is the first run that got past
`Wait for the operator to report Ready`, where the reconcile reported
`0 created, 0 updated, 21 unchanged, 0 deleted` — the claim that blocked three runs now settles as
unchanged, exactly as D-501 predicted.

### F-485 — Piping a long run through tail hid its prompt

> _2026-10-11 · cross-cutting · open_

A cycle run looked hung for twenty-five minutes: no children, an idle event loop, no new pods. It
was not hung at all, it was waiting for a yes/no answer to 'create it with 1 agent node(s)', and the
prompt was invisible because the command was piped through tail — which prints nothing until the
process exits. The lesson is to send a long-lived or interactive command's output to a file and to
close its stdin, so a prompt fails loudly instead of stalling: run it under nohup, with stdin from
/dev/null and the output into a log, then read the log. A second finding from the same run: the
runbook never assumes a cluster (F-446), so with no --cluster it offers to create its own, and one
it creates has none of the integration backends the deploy needs.

### F-514 — A citation can resolve, name the wrong entry, and have nothing behind it

> _2026-10-13 · cross-cutting · open_

The realm sweep read 84 cited ids across 386 sites and found three ways a citation can be wrong
while resolving cleanly. One comment cited F-379, a dockerignore fact, for the separator fact F-395
holds. One cited F-404, a CR-shape friction, for an entry-path fact no entry carried at all — a
reference is a promise that the reasoning is in memory, and that one had nowhere to point, so F-513
was written from the comment and the paragraph moved into it. And 21 sites cited a superseded
decision: where the entry names its successor, which is the Superseded-by line that close --by
writes, the retarget is mechanical and 14 sites were fixed; where it does not name one (D-433,
D-514, D-515) a person has to decide. Two hygiene findings came with it: F-404 and F-405 held the
same friction twice, same title and body, because a batch import had been applied twice and the copy
had collected its own citations, and one prune wrote a ledger heading that the file's own markdown
check rejects. A word-overlap heuristic flagged 39 of the 386 sites, three of them real, so the
audit is reading rather than scoring.

### F-521 — Dropping a devDependency re-resolved supports-color everywhere

> _2026-10-13 · ci · open_

Removing @vscode/test-cli, @vscode/test-electron and @types/mocha from ext/rest-fs, to drop a test
harness whose only test had been deleted, made a plain rush update delete supports-color@10.2.2 from
the lockfile entirely: 1119 peer suffixes flipped from supports-color@10.2.2 to
supports-color@8.1.1, because @vscode/test-cli was the only claimant of version 10 and debug
resolves its optional supports-color peer to the highest version in the graph. The churn reproduced
after reverting the lockfile and re-running a plain rush update, so it was a real re-resolution and
not leftover common-temp state, and a 2500-line diff for removing a test dependency is the
regression F-424 warns about. The fix is to drop the three devDependencies and instead pin
supports-color at ^10.2.2 in the ext/rest-fs package.json itself: that keeps version 10 in the graph
and shrinks the lockfile diff to 3 added and 288 removed lines, all of them the dropped packages.
The lesson is that when a removed dependency is the last claimant of a transitive version, re-add
that version as a direct dependency of the same package rather than keeping the whole dependency or
reaching for common-versions.json.

### F-522 — The cache save costs per file, and CI caches 209k of them

> _2026-10-14 · ci · open_

Run 38593732609 is the measurement that corrects this entry's numbers, and the correction matters
because it changes what the fix is. CI's archive carries 208 877 files in 2.8 GB and its save took
41m22s, while the _restore_ of that same 767 MB archive takes 20s in every job that reads it, a
local `tar` plus `zstd` of the same tree takes 2.8s, and the 271 MB Playwright archive saves in 6s.
The cost is therefore per _file_ — the enumeration, not the bytes — and the same rate shows up in
the `build / audit` job, whose `Upload Audit Results` step globs `**/audit/auditResults.json` and
spends 20m40s walking this workspace for one small file, in this run and in the previous one alike.
The 462 281 figure was this machine's own artifact of a pnpm upgrade: on the runner the store holds
two layout generations, `v11` with 80 549 files and `v12` with 2 626, and none of the older ones, so
pruning there buys nothing. What the archive is made of, measured on the runner: `common/temp` 206
268 files, of which the store is 83 176, `common/temp/node_modules` 98 765 and
`common/temp/install-run` 24 316; the project `node_modules` are 427 files because they are
symlinks, `*/dist` is 2 042 and `*/.rush` is 138. The lesson is to count files rather than bytes
before a tree goes through the cache or an artifact, to keep the archive to a single file by packing
it first, and never to put a `**` glob in front of an upload.

### F-525 — A mis-indented line broke the shared workflow for every caller

> _2026-10-14 · ci · open_

One line's indentation in `rush.yaml` put the setup job's new `audit` output at the job level
instead of inside `outputs:`, which is valid YAML and invalid Actions: every run in this repository,
and in the two others that call `infitx-org/actions/.github/workflows/rush.yaml@main`, failed with
`Invalid workflow file (Line: 81, Col: 5): Unexpected value 'audit'` before a step started. What
would have caught it is a key-set validation rather than a YAML parse — `import yaml` accepts the
file happily, and so did my own verification, which printed the parsed step lists and never looked
at the keys around them. A workflow file has to be checked against the keys Actions accepts at each
level (workflow, job, step), that a step holds exactly one of `uses` or `run`, and that a
`needs.<job>.<output>` reference names an output its target declares; the last of those reports this
fault on its own, because the same line moved the output out of the job that declared it.
`.github/check-workflows.py` in the actions repository is that check and answers in about a second.
The edit itself slipped because the replacement text I wrote carried four spaces of indentation
where the file had six, and the tool matched the four inside the six — a change to a file that three
products call deserves the gate before the push, not after.

### F-526 — A 24-hour release-age policy, not the cache, blocked the install

> _2026-10-14 · ci · open_

Run 38613947575 failed in `Rush Install`, which looks like the cache change and is not: the workflow
parsed, the cache step reported a genuine miss for that lockfile, the unpack printed its documented
fallback, and what failed is pnpm's supply-chain policy —
`[ERR_PNPM_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE_VIOLATION] 2 lockfile entries failed verification` — naming
`@fastify/helmet@13.2.0`, published 2026-10-13T19:28:14Z, and `undici@8.12.1`, published
2026-10-14T09:24:19Z, against a cutoff twenty-four hours before the run. The limit is Rush's default
rather than anything set in this repository, and it is deterministic: deleting
`common/temp/pnpm-store/lockfile-verified.jsonl` and running `rush install` reproduces the same two
packages in ten seconds, and restoring the file makes the install pass again — so the store's own
verification record is what lets a warm machine keep installing, while a cold one, which is what CI
is on every cache miss, re-checks and is refused. The gate clears by itself: `@fastify/helmet` at
19:28Z the same day and `undici` at 09:24Z the next, unless the lockfile is changed first or the
policy is relaxed with `minimumReleaseAgeExclude`. Two consequences worth keeping: while the install
fails no run reaches the pack step, so the packed-store payload stays unmeasured, and the lesson is
to read the failing command before the diff — the error sat three lines below a message naming two
packages and two timestamps.

### F-543 — A suite that dies at load publishes exit 1 and no reason

> _2026-10-16 · ci · open_

Run 618 of Build left four of its seven failed operations with no reason at all.
`realm/blong-access`, `realm/blong-gateway`, `realm/blong-party` and `test/framework` each reported
only `test process exited with code 1` beside `1..0 # no tests found`, and the check that actually
refused them — the unknown-key validation a suite runs while it loads — writes to stderr, which
neither the tap stream the report bundles nor the job log carries.
`blong-dev ci failures --run 618 --full` therefore answered
`unknown — nothing in the evidence points at a cause` four times, and the cause was only recoverable
from the repository itself: the check shipped in c6c07611 (`fix: config validation and hot reload`),
its allow-list was widened in 4789ec10, and `D-554`, `D-555` and `F-527` name the three key shapes
it wrongly refused.

Half of it is fixed. The reading side now uses what the tap runner already captures: `artifacts.ts`
reads `tap-stderr.txt` out of the artifact (`RUNNER_STDERR_FILE` in ci/evidence.ts), and for a
failure whose message is `test process exited with code N` it prefers that slice over the stream,
labelling it `from tap-stderr.txt:`. What remains is the capturing side, and it is the reason this
entry is still open: run 618's artifact had **no** `tap-stderr.txt` although the tap runner writes
one whenever stderr is non-empty, so the refusal never reached the tap process's own stderr — it is
written by the loader the suite spawns, or swallowed by the logger, and finding out which is the
next step before adding a capture. The lesson stands: a module's load failure must leave a reason
the run can publish — either the loader logs the refused key through the log server, or the child's
stderr is kept the way 9abdd6dd made `graceful-shutdown.spawn.test.ts` keep it.

### F-546 — The validation budget depends on the failure, not the tool

> _2026-10-16 · ci · open_

The fidelity variant of the validation — the prompt a user types,
`check the failure in the last build of blong`, no mention of the skill, the command or the run —
was run twice with a fresh subagent. Both loaded the blong-ci skill, both reached for
`blong-dev ci failures` first, both found the three failing operations including the leg-gap the
published bundle misses, and both reported the two expired budgets and the timing-dependent snapshot
with the prior-run comparison. The quality was higher than the analysis that motivated the work.

The cost was not. The plan budgeted four tool calls and two turns against the 35-call baseline; the
runs cost nine and ten calls over five turns, and the explicit-target variant on run 618 cost
thirty-five. Two reasons, and only one of them was a defect: run 622's bundle was published before
the publisher fix, so the reasons still needed a second call with `--full`, and every extra package
in a comparison cost a call of its own (fixed by letting `ci history` take several packages). The
second reason is a property of the failure class rather than of the tool: run 618's failing suites
died while loading, and the message that refused them is in neither the tap stream nor the job log,
so the agent went to git history to reconstruct what the reports could not say (@@F-543). A budget
for this command has to be stated per class of failure — a run the reports describe is one or two
calls, a run whose causes were never captured is archaeology, and the second class is what the
tooling should be judged on next.

Measured again after the flaky rule and the report-contract changes: the green variant
(`was build 621 green?`) took three commands, two of them cross-checks, and answered
`1 flaky test(s), no failure` without inventing one — against roughly twenty calls for the same
prompt before the fix. The reduction came from the tool and not from the prompt, which is the
evidence that a _fix_ shortens a class of question rather than one question: the same measurement on
622's shape has not dropped yet, because its bundle still predates the publisher fix.

Measured again on run 625 — the first red run published after the publisher fix, and the same shape
as 622: one test file killed before it emitted TAP. The publisher half of the fix did land, since
the bundle carries the message and a 23-line excerpt, so the first call alone printed the failing
file, the reason and the raw block, and the extra `--full` call 622 still needed is gone. The cost
did not fall with it: the run took twenty-one terminal commands, because the message read
`test process exited with code unknown` while `signal: SIGILL` — the one field naming the cause
class — sat in the same diagnostics block and was dropped by `tapReport.ts` (@@F-549). That is the
sharpened lesson, and it holds past this command: evidence the tool can print is not a cause it can
state, so the agent returned to the artifacts to recover a field the tool already had. The next
measurement is the same question on the next red run after @@F-549 is fixed.

Measured once more on run 626, the first red run published after @@F-549 was fixed, and the same
question cost eight terminal commands instead of twenty-one. What moved is where the reason came
from: the first `ci failures` call answered `test process exited with signal SIGILL`, so the agent
never left the tool for the field that names the cause class, and the remaining commands were the
diligence the answer invites — `--full` for the stream, `ci history` and `ci runs` for the
comparison, a grep of the test file for what it spawns. That is the measurement the paragraph above
was waiting for: fixing the message moved this shape's cost, where the publisher fix on its own had
only removed one call.

### F-550 — The same kill hit two consecutive runs, unexplained

> _2026-10-16 · ci · open_

Run 626 killed the tap child for tools/blong-ttk/integration.test.ts with SIGILL before it emitted
TAP (`1..0 # no tests found`, `not ok 2`, `exitCode: null`, 15.75s), one run after 625 killed the
child for tools/blong-dev/src/memory/memoryFormat.test.ts the same way — two consecutive red runs,
two different packages, one class, plus a local occurrence the day before (@@F-533). Neither report
says why: tap records only the signal, no artifact captures the killed child's stderr (@@F-543), and
the job log holds no reason, so both diagnoses end at `unknown`. Two lessons.
`1..0 # no tests found` is not a signature by itself — core/blong-gogo and core/blong-mock report it
in every run, green ones included, where it is the empty plan of a file that loaded, registered
nothing and passed; what marks a kill is that phrase beside `not ok` and a signal. And the tool
answers per run, so a recurrence across runs is invisible in it: an agent reading only the default
answer sees one package dying on a signal, not that the previous run died the same way in a
different package.

Measured correlation, added 2026-10-16: commit 00307735 raised the workflow's ci-test-jobs from 2 to
4 on 2026-10-15 14:48, and the per-package test times of unchanged suites tripled at that boundary.
blong-ttk, whose counts are 168 in every one of these runs, went from 4.3 to 7.4 seconds under 2
jobs to 13 to 16 seconds under 4; blong-dev from 51 seconds and 1m33s to 4m27s and 4m34s. The first
run after the change (622) failed on two expired tap budgets, which is what a loaded machine
produces, and the two runs after it (625, 626) died at load with the signal. An earlier reading in
this entry implied the class predated the change because 618 died at load under 2 jobs; that bundle
says `test process exited with code 1` in four packages with 24 failures and 12 of them new, which
is a broken commit rather than a killed child, so the signal variant is only known at 4 jobs — the
concurrency is the leading explanation rather than a bystander, four packages at once with tap's own
per-file concurrency on one runner. What the signal adds is that the trap is native rather than
resource denial, since a Rust component's abort is an illegal instruction and lightningcss ships
such a binary in the tree; the module and its message are still unknown because no artifact captures
the child's stderr (@@F-543). @@T-359 is the investigation.

### F-554 — Dev shell resolves the framework source, CI resolves the built dist

> _2026-10-17 · ci · open_

The dev shell exports NODE_OPTIONS with --conditions=blong-dev (in ~/.bashrc), so locally every
import of @feasibleone/blong resolves to core/blong/types.ts (source). CI sets no such condition, so
Node takes the default condition of the exports map and loads core/blong/dist/types.js. A new
runtime export added to types.ts therefore works locally and fails only in CI. The Build #629
failure read SyntaxError: The requested module '@feasibleone/blong' does not provide an export named
'handlerGroup' at realm/blong-core/adapter/db/handlerGroup.ts:1. Prove the CI path before concluding
anything about a local pass: run the probe with NODE_OPTIONS cleared, e.g. env -u NODE_OPTIONS
node --input-type=module -e "console.log(import.meta.resolve('@feasibleone/blong'))".

### F-575 — Docs check needs Kafka for an unrelated artefact

> _2026-10-18 · docs · open_

blong-dev docs check runs every registered artefact generator. One of them starts blong-commander's
dev server, which waits on Kafka and times out after 60s, and the run ends by reporting an unrelated
stale docs/blong/docs/concepts/layer.md. A page that only adds prose cannot get a green check
without those services, so docs verify (build plus diagrams, images and embeds) is the useful gate
unless the changed artefact is actually one of the register entries.

### F-589 — ci-lint linted the generated CI report

> _2026-10-23 · ci · open_

Running `node --run ci-lint` in a realm that had published a CI report reported 2717 errors, every
one of them inside `.ci-report/publish/allure-main-*.js` — a gitignored bundle of the Allure client
that a run copies into the package. The real errors were invisible behind it, and the count made the
package look broken. The shared eslint config now ignores `.ci-report/**`, beside `.playwright/**`
and `allure-results/**`; a package's own gates must never see a generated artifact.

### F-590 — memory refs skips an untracked package

> _2026-10-23 · ci · open_

A new realm is untracked until its first commit, and `blong-dev memory refs` reads the files git
tracks. Thirty files of `realm/blong-sport` cited memory entries and the audit view showed none of
them, while `--dangling` reported the same total as before they existed, so the check looked clean
for a package it had never read. The tokens are still worth writing bare (a backticked token is an
example, not a citation) — the lesson is that the gate only proves something about files already in
the index, and a package's citations get their first real check after it is added.

### F-593 — memory edit rewrote emphasis in entries it did not touch

> _2026-10-25 · cross-cutting · open_

Editing one entry with `blong-dev memory edit` re-serialises the whole file, and the round trip
turned an underscore-emphasis span in an unrelated entry into asterisks — `memory check` then failed
with MD049 at a line the edit never meant to touch, on a file that had passed moments earlier.
`blong-dev memory format` repaired it in place, so the recovery is one command; the lesson is to run
`memory check` after an edit and to read the diff as a whole-file diff, not as 'my entry changed'.

## Resolved

### F-083 — The workspace markdown validator mis-resolves two link forms

> _2026-09-12 · cross-cutting · resolved_

A cross-file fragment (`./references/textures.md#delivery`) is resolved as a FILE PATH and reports
'File ./references/textures.md#delivery not found', and a same-document anchor (`#variant-contract`)
is likewise resolved against the file system. Both were in the new blong-theme skill; the fix is to
reference the section by name in prose and link the file without a fragment.

A freshly created file is also not yet in the link index, so brand-new reference files report 'not
found' for a while — the same four links resolved cleanly on the next `get_errors` call after an
unrelated edit re-triggered analysis. Do not start moving files around in response to those two
diagnostics.

### F-084 — `[CRITICAL_GUARDRAILS]` headings trip a 'No link definition found' warning

> _2026-09-12 · cross-cutting · resolved_

The bracket style in that heading is parsed as a shortcut reference link, so it raises a markdown
warning. It is a repo-wide convention — 14 skills use it — and it surfaces only for the file that
currently has diagnostics, so it is accepted noise. Do not 'fix' it locally by renaming one skill's
heading and breaking the convention.

### F-085 — `create_and_run_task` cannot write tasks.json in this workspace

> _2026-09-12 · cross-cutting · resolved_

The tool errors with `EACCES … mkdir '/workspaces'` for any `workspaceFolder`. The workaround is to
hand-edit the workspace `.vscode/tasks.json` with a file edit and run the task with `run_task`, then
revert the file.

### F-106 — The scaffolded browser orchestrator folder stays literally `subject`

> _2026-08-21 · cross-cutting · resolved_

Do not replace `subject` with the realm name in `browser/orchestrator/subject/init.ts`. The
guardrail is stated in blong-realm, blong-layer and the shared conventions, and in the template file
comments: the scaffolded folder name stays literal and only the `namespace` value is the realm name.

### F-107 — Models are public by default; override only the operation that differs

> _2026-08-21 · cross-cutting · resolved_

Agents were writing manual validations for every operation, so blong-model now states the decision
rule: models are `public: true` by default, and only the differing operation gets an explicit
`gateway/<subject>/<method>.ts` validation. The template ships a public model plus an override
example. The rule is deliberately not universal — the master-detail case (an invoice with `lines`)
is still a separate work item for auto-modelling.

### F-108 — A realm-local orchestrator replaced blong-server's subject orchestrator

> _2026-08-21 · cross-cutting · resolved_

Agents kept creating `orchestrator/$subjectDispatch.ts` and a realm-local `adapter/db.ts` instead of
reusing blong-server. The `[REUSE_SERVER]` guardrail was added to the shared conventions,
blong-realm, blong-layer and `copilot-instructions.md`, and the kopi template no longer ships either
file: it scaffolds `orchestrator/subject/init.ts` (namespace only) and reuses blong-server's
`srv.db`.

### F-109 — Skills disagreed with the code about where the server test layer lives

> _2026-08-21 · cross-cutting · resolved_

Skills and the shared conventions now match `WELL_KNOWN_LAYERS` in `core/blong-gogo/src/load.ts`:
server tap tests live in `server/test/`, browser tap tests in `browser/test/`, and the top-level
`test/` folder is the Playwright (browser) layer. The template scaffolds `server/test/` plus
`browser/test/`. The `docs/blong/docs` pages still need the same alignment — deferred.

### F-110 — A helper file sitting in a handler group raises a loader warning

> _2026-08-21 · cross-cutting · resolved_

blong-handler documents the convention: a helper used by handlers in the same group may live beside
them (the `Watch.ts` warning is benign), shared helpers belong in a `lib/` group, and a `_` or `.`
prefix marks plain files.

### F-111 — The `db_invoice` synthetic-handler naming rabbit hole

> _2026-08-18 · cross-cutting · resolved_

`[DB_ACCESS]` and blong-handler now state plainly that database persistence handlers live in
`adapter/db/` and read `this.config?.context?.queryBuilder`, and the template ships the canonical
`adapter/db/$subject$ObjectAdd.ts`. Time was lost inventing subject-suffixed handler names such as
`db_invoice` before realising there was nothing to invent.

### F-112 — Over-exploration of reference realms before scaffolding a new one

> _2026-08-21 · cross-cutting · resolved_

In the run that cost the most, the agent explored existing realms at length before building
anything. blong-realm is now kopi-first ('scaffold, then adjust'), lists the recommended skill set,
and the blong-kopi README explains how to use the tooling, so the scaffold is trusted instead of
re-explored.
