> _2026-08-21 · cross-cutting · resolved_

blong-core documents non-dotted handler names as the default (`invoiceInvoiceAdd`) and dotted forms
as discouraged special cases, and the template seed uses the non-dotted form. Verifying the rule
against `access.authorization.list` expectations remains a follow-up.

### F-114 — Audit columns must be nullable or the gateway rejects the write

> _2026-08-18 · cross-cutting · resolved_

blong-schema carries an `[AUTO_VALIDATION]` guardrail: server-managed audit fields must be nullable
(`createdAt: type.dateTimeNull()`), because the gateway auto-validates CRUD params against the
table's `NotNull` columns. The template schema demonstrates the convention with a comment.

### F-116 — A stale editor error that a clean `tsc` run disproves

> _2026-09-10 · cross-cutting · resolved_

`get_errors` reported a stale `Property 'retry' does not exist on type '{}'` on `knex.ts(384)` long
after `tsc -p tsconfig.json` had passed with exit 0. The language-server cache lags multi-file type
edits: `types.ts` had gained `retry`, but the Problems panel was still holding an old module graph.

When the Problems panel disagrees with a clean package `tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json` run, trust
the `tsc` run. Do not chase phantom errors by changing code that compiles.

### F-117 — A folder-only refactor broke paths a text grep could never see

> _2026-09-10 · cross-cutting · resolved_

Moving `eslint` to `tools/eslint` left 25 `eslint.config.mjs` files importing
`../eslint/config.mjs`; `tools/blong-graph/tsconfig.json` extended a sibling tsconfig by relative
path; and `common/git-hooks/pre-commit` invoked `core/blong-dev/bin/blong-dev.ts` by path. Each of
the three classes was found only by running the tooling, because a grep for `core/<pkg>` matches
none of them.

`rush build` had already passed clean, which made the breakage look impossible: `eslint.config.mjs`
is not part of any build graph, so lint was the only thing that could catch it, and `blong-dev lint`
failing on one package masked the rest.

After moving packages run `rush ci-lint` and `rush build`, and grep for `../<pkg>` as well as
`core/<pkg>`. A green build is not evidence for a path-only refactor.

### F-118 — A trailing comma in `tsconfig.json` looked like a path-mapping bug

> _2026-09-10 · cross-cutting · resolved_

An edit added a trailing comma where the original JSON line had none, in
`tools/blong-graph/tsconfig.json`. The malformed config made TypeScript fall back to the base
config's `rootDir` and emit a cascade of TS6059 errors that read like a broken path mapping; the
decisive clue came from `blong-dev lint`, which reported `Parsing error: Unexpected token RBrace`.

After editing JSON or JSONC, re-read or parse the file to confirm punctuation before drawing
conclusions from downstream errors.

### F-119 — `tap` compiles with the package tsconfig, so it needs `ts-node` and node types

> _2026-09-12 · cross-cutting · resolved_

`tap` transpiles with the package's `tsconfig.json`, which makes two omissions fatal in ways that
`node file.ts` never shows. A new package tsconfig with `outDir` but no
`ts-node: {transpileOnly: true, swc: true}` block made tap fail with TS5011
(`The common source directory ... must have rootDir set`) or with an opaque
`Debug Failure. Output generation failed`; copying the `blong-kopi` template's `ts-node` section
fixed it. A tsconfig that omits `types: ["node"]` cannot resolve `node:*` or `process` even though
`@types/node` is installed — `core/blong-lib` only got away with it because it never imports a node
builtin.

Keep a package's tsconfig aligned with the `blong-kopi` template whenever the package is created or
its build settings change.

### F-145 — Edit anchors failed on text inferred from a summary instead of read

> _2026-09-12 · cross-cutting · resolved_

Three edit anchors failed on text that had been inferred rather than read: the box-drawing `// ──`
runs, and a doc comment assumed to be wrapped over two lines that was on one. Read the exact lines
before editing, and do not reconstruct them from a summary.

### F-146 — A fast `tap` subset run needs different flags

> _2026-09-14 · cross-cutting · resolved_

`tap` 21 in this repo rejects `--no-coverage` with `Unknown option`. For a fast subset run use
`--allow-incomplete-coverage --coverage-report=none` and ignore the resulting 'incomplete' ERROR
lines, which are an artifact of running a subset rather than a real coverage gap.

### F-147 — Four independent CI causes behind three apparently unrelated failures

> _2026-09-15 · ci · resolved_

The CI failures looked like three unrelated problems — a `blong-kukum` e2e assertion, a
`semantic-log` suite 'failure' and a flaky realm test — and were four independent causes: a regex
assertion reading console text the runner no longer prints, tap's `failures` counter counting skips,
a hidden-folder artifact upload, and tap's own configuration leaking into a nested run.

### F-148 — A nested `tap` run ignores `--reporter=json` and reports zero tests

> _2026-09-15 · ci · resolved_

`blong-kukum`'s e2e suite runs the fixture realm from inside its own tap process, so the nested tap
inherited `TAP_CHILD_ID` and `TAP_JOB_ID`, concluded it was a child of the outer run and printed
plain TAP. The symptom was maximally misleading: `blong-dev test` exited 0, printed no summary line
and wrote a report with zero tests, which reads like a reporting bug — three hypotheses died first
(spawnSync versus shell, stale 'first run after regeneration' state, a stale Playwright report
overwriting the tap one) because each was plausible and none was checked against the raw child
output.

What found it was dumping the raw artifact and the environment: `blong-dev test` writes its unparsed
stream to `.ci-report/tap.json`, and dumping `process.env` from inside a tap process named the cause
in one line. `mimic.mjs`, which spawns the fixture run exactly as the e2e does from a plain node
script, passed while the e2e failed, which proves the difference is the context (inside tap) rather
than the command.

Dump the raw artifact and the environment before forming a fourth hypothesis about the code under
test, and write the cheaper reproduction — a throwaway tap file that spawns and dumps — before the
third run of a 3-minute suite.

### F-193 — One portal can only be configured by one handler

> _2026-09-17 · cross-cutting · resolved_

Loading a second realm that answers portalConfigGet into realm/blong-gateway replaced that realm own
model-driven menu, and all thirteen of its own specs timed out waiting for portal-menu-gateway - one
child entry, thirteen failures. blong-commander and blong-realm each answer portalConfigGet for
their own pages, so a suite that loads two such realms loses one of the menus. Lesson: before adding
a page-owning realm to another realm, check which handler wins the portal config, and treat the
other realm own suite as the evidence.

orchestrator/portal/portalConfigMerge.ts merges every portalConfigGet provider via
mergePortalConfigs, and portalMerge.play.ts proves two menus compose

### F-225 — tap 30s subprocess default is smaller than an integration file startup

> _2026-09-21 · ci · resolved_

realm/blong-access failed CI with a single `timeout!` failure and 52 tests passing, which reads as a
hung suite. Running the same file locally took 25.9s, and instrumenting it showed where the time
goes: 13.5s of `load()` (both platforms through the runtime) before any test runs, 0.5s of
`start()`, 2.7s of tests, 2.3s of `stop()`.

tap's default is 30 seconds for the subprocess, and it is the same number tap hands the child as the
per-test timeout, so one budget answers two questions. `--timeout` takes **seconds**, which tap's
own source comment ("timeout in ms for test subprocesses") contradicts: `--timeout=1` reproduces the
CI failure exactly, while `--timeout=20000` does nothing at all.

Lesson: a tap file whose fixed startup dominates its runtime is judged against a budget it cannot
see, and `timeout!` names the failure after the mechanism rather than the cause — measure the phases
before believing a suite hung.

Fixed by D-247: blong-dev test passes --timeout=180 unless the invocation sets its own.
realm/blong-access now runs its 52 tap tests green in ~26s, and --timeout=1 still reproduces the CI
failure, so the override path works.

### F-287 — A committed dark diagram was unreadable because the theme owns the label colour

> _2026-09-27 · docs · resolved_

The first two posts of the 2026 series were rendered and verified, and both renders loaded in the
built site, so every check the repo had said the diagrams were fine: docs verify counts the diagrams
that drew and the images that loaded, and it cannot see a colour. Mermaid paints label text from the
theme, so the style directive that set fill:#e8f4ff for emphasis left the text to the dark
theme's #ccc and the words on those nodes measured 1.44:1 for a dark-mode reader while the same SVG
was perfect in light mode. The lesson is that an image is only verified when its pixels are reasoned
about, not when it loads: the fix is a rule (a fill must carry its own color, at 4.5:1 or better)
enforced by blong-dev mermaid check, which measures the source and the rendered SVG, and runs in
ci-docs.

Fixed by the colour rule and by blong-dev mermaid check, which measures both the source and the
render.

### F-288 — A committed diagram image was invented before the house convention was read

> _2026-09-27 · docs · resolved_

The first five blog posts were written with a light and dark SVG pair and a playbook to render it,
because the plan asked every post to ship an image and a static image was assumed to need its own
palette. The docs site already answers this: a diagram written into the page is rendered by the site
with the reader's theme, which is why every other page embeds mermaid and nobody maintains a diagram
palette. Building the renderer, the contrast rule, the unit tests and the ci-docs step took most of
a session and then had to be removed again, and the static render it produced was the only artefact
in the series that could be unreadable without any check noticing. Lesson: read how the site renders
the artefact type before inventing tooling for it, and prefer the surface that inherits the theme
over the one that has to be told the colours.

Resolved by removing the renderer and the pairs: the posts embed mermaid, and docs verify now covers
the blog.

### F-289 — A greedy scripted replacement deleted three plan sections with no git history

> _2026-09-27 · docs · resolved_

A python replacement that took its start index at a new subsection and its end index at the next arc
heading swallowed everything between them: the Where the posts go, Publishing and The series at a
glance sections, the 36-post table and the Preparing a missing or partial doc subsection, about 90
lines. plans/ is untracked, so git could not restore it and the text survived only in the session
transcript and was written back by hand. Lesson: index-based slicing in a script is a delete with
extra steps, so anchor on a unique string with a try-asserted count, prefer the edit tool for a
large removal, and treat a document that git does not track as one where a bad edit is
unrecoverable.

The lesson was correct and insufficient on its own: what stops the third occurrence is the rule in
the file being edited, plus keeping a copy of a document git does not track. F-292 carries the
second incident and the rule.

### F-303 — The repo formats markdown with a prettier the packages do not have

> _2026-09-28 · cross-cutting · resolved_

Running the prettier binary from a package node_modules reformatted whole markdown files (it is v2
with a different trailing-comma and prose default than the config assumes, so list markers and
paragraph wraps changed everywhere), and it reported a different file as unformatted than the pinned
formatter does. The repository pins prettier v3 under common/, and the format rush command uses that
one, so use it rather than a package copy. A second trap: prettier takes .gitignore as an ignore
path in addition to .prettierignore, so checking copies placed under a gitignored folder such as
dev/ silently matches zero files and prints the all-clean line. Baseline a formatting question
against the file in its real path, never against a copy under an ignored directory.

Resolved as guidance: the two traps are now recorded, and the changes made after the discovery were
checked with the pinned prettier on the files in place.

### F-241 — Markdown edits need prettier before markdownlint passes

> _2026-09-23 · docs · resolved_

blong-dev lint --files marks a hand-written markdown table with MD060 (table pipes must align with
the header, style aligned) and MD049 (emphasis must be underscore, not asterisk), neither of which
is obvious while editing. The fix for the alignment rule is to run the repo's prettier shim
(rush-prettier, installed under common/temp) with --write on the file, so the order is: edit,
prettier, then lint.

blong-dev lint --fix now runs prettier (the pinned rush-prettier autoinstaller), then
markdownlint --fix, then prettier again, so the edit-prettier-lint order is one command; the memory
pattern page was rewritten with it and the diff stayed at 44 insertions with no unrelated rewraps

### F-467 — A mask hides a wrong shot; redaction showed one

> _2026-10-10 · ci · resolved_

A masked cell turns a wrong screenshot into a stable one, which is how the commander's
`explore-kafka-messages.png` sat in the repository for as long as it did showing the topic list: the
walk accepted the table it had not left, the filter matched nothing, and the magenta `offset` box
hid a cell that held a topic name — so the shot passed in CI and locally while documenting a level
nobody reached. Redacting the value instead of painting the cell is what exposed it, because the
table it belongs to is then visible; the same rewrite of the pod-size and keycloak columns made
their headers, their shape and their place in the table legible. The lesson is to reach for a mask
only when the whole element is noise, and to treat a mask over a value whose _frame_ is meaningful
as a sign the shot is hiding something.

The wrong shot is gone: the kafka messages step reaches its level and the remaining commander
columns redact the value rather than painting it, so what a shot shows is now the table it claims to
show.

### F-471 — The e2e wait step hides its reason in the diagnostics artifact

> _2026-10-10 · ci · resolved_

Two rounds went into the kustomize e2e's `Wait for the operator to report Ready`, and both times the
answer was one line of the custom resource it polls: `phase: Failed` with
`message: '1 step(s) failed, first: <kind>/<namespace>/<name>'`. The failing step is a bare poll
loop, so its log says only that the operator never reported Ready, and the line lives in the
diagnostics artifact instead. The first round found the service objects were never listed in their
own namespace; the second, one round later, found the apply replacing a bound
`PersistentVolumeClaim` with a manifest that dropped the `volumeName` the API assigned when it
bound, refused with status 422. Neither was in the code the failure was attributed to, and neither
would have been found without the artifact — which makes the real lesson that the artifact is the
_first_ place to look when a wait fails, not the last: the resource being waited on already knows
why, and the step could say so itself (a todo in the `ci` area asks for exactly that).

Addressed by T-317: the wait step now prints the status it polls (message first, then the resource)
and fails fast on Failed, so the reason no longer lives only in the diagnostics artifact.

### F-376 — Rush deploy honours .npmignore, a deployment is not a publish

> _2026-10-05 · cross-cutting · resolved_

rush deploy applies the .npmignore filter unless the scenario sets includeNpmIgnoreFiles, whose name
reads backwards: true disables the filter and the default applies it. The repository templates
ignore every file and un-ignore a short list, so a module that no entry point outside its own
package names never reaches the deploy tree. The framework image died on
@feasibleone/semantic-log/attachable.ts, and the suite artifact was missing
realm/blong-kustomize/plan.ts and its siblings, realm/blong-login/server.ts and core/blong/knex.ts,
none of which anything failed on until a pod imported it. Both scenarios now set
includeNpmIgnoreFiles true, which is the rule to copy into a new scenario, and a scanner that
compares a packed artifact against the source tree found every remaining hole in one pass.

Closed as the deploy half, which is fixed and verified: all three scenarios set
includeNpmIgnoreFiles true, the framework image and both artifacts build from an unfiltered tree,
and a dev-cluster cycle fills a node and starts the suite. What the entry could not say is that the
ignore files were never wrong only for deploys: the same allow-lists decide what npm receives, and
four of the seven packages that declare ci-publish ship without their declared entry points, two of
them empty on the registry (F-488, with the fix left as T-322).

### F-488 — The publish allow-lists release packages without their entry points

> _2026-10-11 · cross-cutting · resolved_

rush deploy and npm pack read the same file, but only one of them is described by it. Every
published package carries a .npmignore that ignores everything and un-ignores a compiled layout:
bin, lib, dist, CHANGELOG. Nothing in this repository compiles TypeScript and every consumer imports
the sources through an exports map that names index.ts, so that allow-list keeps build output nobody
produces and drops the code everybody imports. Measured with npm pack --dry-run and confirmed
against the registry: @feasibleone/blong-login@1.12.0 and @feasibleone/blong-openapi@1.2.1 are three
files each, metadata only, an empty package; @feasibleone/blong@1.32.0 is thirteen files of
untracked dist plus types.ts, with no index.ts and no knex.ts; @feasibleone/semantic-log@1.4.0
carries 94 files including every test but omits attachable.ts and capability.ts, two of the five
entry points its own exports map declares, and the first of those is what core/blong-gogo imports
and what started F-376 on the deploy side. What a tarball contains depends on untracked build output
happening to be present in the publishing checkout, which is why two of them are empty. Nobody
notices because every resolution inside this repository goes through the workspace, so the published
packages are only ever consumed from the outside.

Fixed on both halves. The four whitelists that hid entry points now name them: semantic-log gained
attachable.ts and capability.ts (the subpath blong-gogo imports), and the realm-shaped packages
gained their sources, so blong-login packs 31 files where it packed 3, blong-openapi 22 where it
packed 16, blong-test 27 where it packed 20. Eight files that served no publish purpose are deleted
— blong-allure, blong-graph, blong-ttk, blong-kustomize, blong-realm, dev, and the kukum e2e-realm
fixture — while blong-kopi's is kept deliberately because that package may start publishing, and
that list was confirmed before anything was removed. The check that found the defect is committed as
blong-dev publish check, with a unit test of the reader and a repo-level gate in the same suite, and
it fails on a fixture whose whitelist hides a declared subpath. Residual findings are T-323: the
declared targets under dist/ exist only after a build, and blong-openapi declares a browser half it
does not have.

### F-535 — A relative img src in JSX is not an asset the build copies

> _2026-10-15 · docs · resolved_

Docusaurus copies an image into the build only when something imports it: a markdown reference goes
through webpack and lands in `assets/images/` under a hashed name, while a plain relative src in JSX
(poster="./img/editor-toolbar.png") asks for a path the build never wrote, so the poster 404s and
the reader gets a broken-image icon. Pass the import instead —
poster={require('./img/editor-toolbar.png').default} — which is what the component's JSDoc, the
Storybook pattern doc and the blong-docs skill now say. The first `blong-dev docs verify` run over
the new embeds reported exactly this (image did not load), which is the check to trust over a
browser glance.

### F-534 — docusaurus serve drops the query from an iframe URL

> _2026-10-15 · docs · resolved_

`docusaurus serve` — which docs/blong used to run as `npm run serve` — rewrites URLs to clean ones:
a Storybook frame URL such as the iframe entry point with its id query becomes a query-less path,
and the `/storybook/<name>/` directory URL loses its trailing slash. The first loses the story id,
so the preview renders its "No Preview" notice; the second makes a published Storybook's relative
module imports resolve one directory above where they live, so every manager bundle 404s (measured:
/storybook/sb-manager/globals-runtime.js is 404 where
/storybook/browser/sb-manager/globals-runtime.js is 200). It cost a debugging cycle because it looks
like a broken embed: the page was right, the component was right, the server was rewriting the URL.
The dev server (`npm start`) serves the same URLs untouched and a static host does too. Fixed by
pointing docs/blong's `npm run serve` at `blong-dev docs serve` @@D-559; the Docusaurus one stays as
`npm run serve:docusaurus`.

### F-539 — A red run's bundle names fewer legs than the run

> _2026-10-16 · ci · resolved_

The red run 622 of Build published `totals.packages: 2` and neither failure carried a message, while
the run's own summary block named three failing operations. blong-log failed its storybook leg (an
image snapshot) and is published as passed, because only the tap, vitest and Playwright legs write
`.ci-report/report.json` and that file is all the bundle reads; the storybook leg leaves
`storybook.log` and an exit code. The two entries that are present are tap's own words —
`tap exited with code 1 without reporting a failing test` and `timeout!` — which name the verdict
and not what was running when the budget ran out. The reason is in the raw stream: `tap.raw.tap`
beside each report, where the last emitted assertion and tap's `expired: index.test.ts` line show
which budget expired and where. Fetch it from the run's `reports` artifact with `gh run download`;
the published per-package page renders the same report the bundle already had, so it adds nothing.

Resolved: the storybook leg reports a slice of its own into .ci-report, so a failing leg decides the
package status and reaches the bundle with the jest message; the raw tap stream is still where a
timeout is read.

### F-540 — An in-file tap timeout undercuts the runner's budget

> _2026-10-16 · ci · resolved_

`blong-dev test` passes `--timeout=240` so that a tap entry point is never judged by a budget
smaller than its own startup (@@D-247), and both files that failed in run 622 replace that budget at
runtime: `t.setTimeout(60_000)` in `demo/blong-cli/index.test.ts`, `tap.setTimeout(60_000)` in
`core/blong-kukum/index.test.ts`. tap hands one number to the root test and to its children, so the
expiry lands in the middle of the file rather than isolating a hang: blong-cli expired after four of
its five tests and 51.6s of spawned CLI runs, and kukum's gateway test ended at 60044ms while
`kukum.source.check` — a package-wide lint run for a request that names one file — was still going.
Both files had passed on the previous run at 26.7s and 1m50s, and took 70s and 5m43s in this one, so
the in-file 60s is a budget a loaded shared runner crosses rather than a ceiling only a hang
reaches.

Resolved: the in-file setTimeout ceilings are gone from both test files, so the budget the runner
passes applies instead.

### F-542 — A storybook snapshot reason still classifies as unknown

> _2026-10-16 · ci · resolved_

Diagnosing run 622 for the blong-log package: the storybook leg failed on a LogViewer image snapshot
diff (0.527% differing pixels) and `blong-dev ci failures --full` printed the excerpt correctly but
still classified the leg as `unknown — nothing in the evidence points at a cause`. The blong-ci
skill's own table names a storybook image snapshot diff as timing-dependent, so the classifier has
the vocabulary for this reason and did not apply it; a reader gets `unknown` where the answer is
available. The lesson is that the leg-gap path (a leg publishing no report, read from the leg's log)
may bypass the snapshot rule the single-leg path applies. Verify by rerunning `--full` on 622 and
checking whether the verdict differs for a leg whose reason came from the storybook runner rather
than from TAP.

Fixed in the same change: classify.ts now reads the tolerated diff out of the message or the excerpt
and returns snapshot-mismatch with the percentage and pixel count, so a leg whose reason came from
its own log no longer reads as unknown (verdict kind snapshot-mismatch in ci/types.ts, cases in
ci/classify.test.ts).

### F-544 — A flaky retry makes a green run look red

> _2026-10-16 · ci · resolved_

Build 621 was green and every tool in the chain agreed except the one built to answer the question.
`gh run view 38750588310` reports conclusion success, all ten jobs succeeded and the first attempt
was the only one; the run's reports artifact holds 34 `.ci-report/report.json` files with
`failed: 0` between them, and one entry whose status is `flaky` (`realm/blong-party`, playwright
`profile.play.ts`, whose published `summary.json` says `status: passed` with `retries: 1`).
`blong-dev ci failures --run 621` nevertheless printed `Build #621 · 3803c5d9 · red`, because
`isProblem` counts flaky, so `collectFailures` puts the retried test in the failure list,
`buildFailuresBundle` returns null only for an empty list, and `diagnose.ts` derives `red` from
`observed.tests > 0`. Two consequences cost the investigation: the premise stated in `site.ts` and
in the blong-ci skill — that a green run publishes no bundle — is false, so the presence of
`failures/<workflow>/<n>/failures.json` is not evidence of a red run; and the command's own
interpretation table calls a flaky status not a failure while its verdict line calls the run red.
Trust the run's own conclusion, and read the bundle's `totals.failed` rather than its existence.

Fixed: red in ci/diagnose.ts is now a failed test or a failed operation, a bundle whose only entries
are flaky is reported as N flaky test(s), no failure with a note saying why the bundle exists, and
the claim in ci/site.ts and in the blong-ci skill no longer says a green run publishes no bundle.
Run 621 is a fixture in ci/diagnose.test.ts.

### F-545 — ci history cannot read a package page Allure replaced

> _2026-10-16 · ci · resolved_

`blong-dev ci history blong-party` printed one run, #618, although the site holds a blong-party page
for 618 through 622. The pages for 619, 620, 621 and 622 are Allure reports (their title is Allure
Report – Pull request #200), because a package whose tests report to Allure publishes that report in
the page's place, and `packagePage.ts` can only read its own `blong-package-summary` script tag.
History therefore appears to end five runs back, and the `prior` line of a diagnosis named a stale
run: for run 621 it named 618, whose blong-party record is a one-test failure.

Half of it is fixed: the comparison a diagnosis makes no longer needs the page. `comparisonReader`
in commands/ci.ts asks for the page first and falls back to the run's failure bundle, which answers
whether the package was red (and nothing about how long it took), so the `prior` line names the run
before it rather than a run five back, and the comparison says when it came from the bundle. What
remains is the `history` verb itself, which prints nothing for a package whose runs published Allure
pages: either read the Allure document (its embedded summary or `widgets/summary.json`) or publish
the package summary beside it.

Fixed on both sides: the published directory now carries package-summary.json, written by the page
renderer and by the Allure publish path alike, and site.ts reads it before the page and before the
run's bundle, so a package whose runs publish Allure pages is comparable again — and for the fifteen
runs already published the page-or-bundle fallbacks still apply. ci history takes several packages
in one call too.

### F-555 — CI tests run against a dist cached under a lockfile-only key

> _2026-10-17 · ci · resolved_

The shared Rush workflow (infitx-org/actions) caches every project's dist in the same archive as the
pnpm store, under a key that hashes only common/config/rush/pnpm-lock.yaml. setup restores that key,
runs rush rebuild and creates a correct dist, but an exact key hit suppresses the archive save, so
the cache keeps serving the dist of whatever commit first wrote that key. The tests job (needs:
setup) restores the same archive, runs rush install and the suites without a rebuild, so it tests
against that stale framework build. Build #629 died this way: a handlerGroup export added to
core/blong/types.ts was in neither the cached core/blong/dist/types.js nor the type-only code path.
Any change to a runtime export or runtime logic in types.ts is invisible to CI until the lockfile
changes. The fix belongs in the workflow: carry the dist as a per-run artifact (or under a
per-commit key) instead of inside the lockfile-keyed dependency archive.

Fixed on 2026-10-17 in infitx-org/actions: the lockfile-keyed archive carries dependencies and the
per-project .rush trees only, and the job that runs rush rebuild packs every dist tree into
common/temp/build.tar.zst and uploads it as the build artifact of the run, which each job that reads
the tree downloads and unpacks. Verified by rebuilding core/blong/dist locally and running the
blong-access and blong-gateway suites with NODE_OPTIONS cleared: 70/70 and 21/21 through the same
resolution CI uses.

### F-597 — The k3d Kafka broker OOMs and looks like a broken port mapping

> _2026-10-25 · cross-cutting · resolved_

The local k3d broker is OOMKilled about every four hours at its 512Mi memory limit (39 restarts in
two weeks), and the container keeps no volume, so each restart loses the topic and the postStart
hook recreates and re-seeds it. A commander explore run that lands in that window fails the whole
webServer with node-rdkafka `Local: Broker transport failure`, which looks like a broken port
mapping: the k3d port 9092 is exposed and open, and the broker answers `kafka-topics` from inside
the pod throughout. Check `kubectl describe pod -l app=kafka` for
`Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled` before touching ports, wait for the rollout, and read
the topic's offsets with `kafka-get-offsets` before re-seeding by hand. CI is unaffected — a fresh
cluster on every run — so the limit stays as it is and the lesson is local-only.

No change: the OOM is local-only (CI runs a fresh cluster) and the limit stays. The diagnostic order
— describe the pod for OOMKilled, wait for the rollout, then read offsets — is the part worth
keeping.
